title: Free Because You Want It
objective: After this level you can explain compatibilism, the view of Hobbes and Hume that freedom means acting on your own wants, not escaping causes, using Hobbes's water flowing down its channel.
summary: Compatibilists Hobbes and Hume held that freedom is doing what you will unimpeded, like water in its channel; van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument replies.

cards.headline: Is a river free as it runs downhill?
cards.body: It can’t flow uphill. Yet nothing is stopping it. In Leviathan (1651), Thomas Hobbes thought that picture dissolved the free will problem.

cards.headline: Freedom means no stop
cards.body: Compatibilists hold that free will and determinism can both be true. The classic version comes from Hobbes and Hume: freedom is doing what you will without external impediment. Hobbes said a free man finds “no stop” in doing what he has the will, desire or inclination to do. Chains take away your freedom. Your own wanting doesn’t, even if your wanting has causes.

cards.headline: Water in its channel
cards.body: Hobbes gave the image: “Liberty and Necessity are Consistent: As in the water, that hath not only Liberty, but a Necessity of descending by the Channel.” Your voluntary actions come from your will, so they are free. Every act of will has causes in a continual chain, so they are also necessary. Free and caused at once, like the river.

cards.headline: Hume: only prisoners lack it
cards.body: In his Enquiry (1748), Hume called the whole quarrel merely verbal. Liberty, he wrote, is simply “a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will”. If you choose to stay put, you may; if you choose to move, you may. That liberty, he said, belongs to everyone “who is not a prisoner and in chains”.

cards.headline: The Consequence Argument
cards.body: Incompatibilists aren’t convinced. Peter van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument runs: if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws of nature and of events before we were born. Neither of those is up to us. So our acts aren’t up to us either. Many compatibilists think it unsound, but it set their agenda: they owe it a reply.

cards.headline: Free Because You Want It: the big picture
learned: Compatibilists: free will and determinism can both be true
Hobbes: freedom is finding no stop
Water has liberty and necessity at once
Van Inwagen: our acts aren’t up to us if determined

questions.prompt: Which image did Hobbes use to show that liberty and necessity are consistent?

options.label: A bird in an open cage
A ship steered by its captain
A clock wound by its maker

questions.explanation: Hobbes’s water has both liberty and a necessity of descending by the channel, as voluntary actions are both free and caused.

questions.prompt: Why did Hobbes and Hume think a fully caused world leaves freedom intact?

options.label: Free acts, they said, have no causes of any kind at all
options.rationale: That’s closer to the libertarian view.

options.label: Freedom is acting on your will unimpeded, not escaping causes
Strong enough willpower can break the laws of nature
Nobody can ever predict what anyone will decide to do

questions.explanation: For classical compatibilists, freedom is the absence of external impediments to doing what you will, which determinism doesn’t remove.

questions.prompt: The Daodejing in Level 7 and Hobbes both use water. What is it a picture of for each?

options.label: Daodejing: acting without forcing; Hobbes: freedom that is also necessary
Daodejing: freedom that is also necessary; Hobbes: acting without forcing
Both: the chaos of a world without laws
Both: the soul flowing out of the body

questions.explanation: The Daodejing’s water models wu wei, acting without forcing; Hobbes’s water in its channel shows liberty and necessity together.
